claim: Ketamine is a non-competitive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist.
source: The discovery of ketamine, a non-competitive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist as a rapid-acting antidepressant, inspired extensive research to understand the mechanisms of ketamine's action as well as a new perspective on the neurobiology of depression that depression might reflect non-adaptive changes in the glutamatergic and GABA (gamma aminobutyric acid)-ergic signal transmission of the prefrontal and limbic system in response to environmental stress and adversity (Berman et al., 2000; Zarate et al., 2006; Sanacora et al., 2008; Lapidus et al., 2014; Krystal et al., 2013; Abdallah et al., 2015; Duman et al., 2016; Murrough et al., 2017; Krystal et al., 2019; Duman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a known property of ketamine, supported by multiple citations.

evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Depression might reflect non-adaptive changes in the glutamatergic and GABA-ergic signal transmission of the prefrontal and limbic system in response to environmental stress and adversity.

claim: In control sessions where saline was administered, animals tended to repeat the choice that yielded a token, while switching away from the choice that led to non-gain outcomes.
source: In the control sessions where saline was administered, animals tended to repeat the choice that yielded a token, while switching away from the choice that led to non-gain outcomes, with a stronger tendency to switch after loss than neutral outcome (i.e. zero token) (Equation 1; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, shown in Figure 1C and modeled by Equation 1.

claim: Animals had a stronger tendency to switch after loss than neutral outcome.
source: In the control sessions where saline was administered, animals tended to repeat the choice that yielded a token, while switching away from the choice that led to non-gain outcomes, with a stronger tendency to switch after loss than neutral outcome (i.e. zero token) (Equation 1; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The reinforcing and punishing effects of gain and non-gain outcomes decayed exponentially over time, with the recent outcomes exerting a larger effect than remote ones.
source: The reinforcing and punishing effects of gain and non-gain outcomes also decayed exponentially over time, with the recent outcomes exerting a larger effect than remote ones.

claim: The ketamine-induced modulation was larger for the effect of recent than remote outcomes.
source: In addition, the ketamine-induced modulation was larger for the effect of recent than remote outcomes (analysis of variance [ANOVA], three-way interaction among outcome, trial lag, and drug condition, F(8, 1964) = 4.05, F(8, 1649) = 4.46, and F(8, 509) = 3.62 for animal P, Y, and B, respectively. p < 0.001 in all animals for IM administration of 0.5 mg/kg; F(8, 1229) = 4.89, p < 0.001 in animal P; F(8, 389) = 1.89, p = 0.06 in Y; F(8, 1002) = 3.27, p = 0.001 in B for IN administration of 1 mg/kg).

claim: Ketamine did not significantly modulate the time constant of decay.

claim: Under ketamine, value update increased positively following all outcomes, thus increasing overall probability of repeating the same choice.

claim: As the animals owned more tokens and were closer to earning juice reward, fixation errors became less frequent under ketamine.

claim: Animals could counter the undesirable effect of ketamine on fixation when they had stronger motivation to obtain juice reward.
